title: Lightbulb Moment: Big Business Needs “mini-Edisons” To Drive Invention
text:
With artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI, sweeping the world, we are experiencing a new era of founder-inventors - a new "Gründerzeit," as the Germans call the last decades of the 19th century when inventions like modern railway systems, modern finance, and the automobile transformed society.
Today, a wave of inventions are appearing overnight, sprouting like mushrooms from recent advancements in AI and led by founder-inventors whose names will go down in history as did their predecessors like von Siemens, Edison, Pasteur and Benz.
In such an era, how do established companies keep up?
The upstarts are founded by visionary individuals who are willing to take risks and challenge the status quo. But established companies are often hindered by legacy systems, outdated thinking, and a fear of failure. What’s needed is some corporate therapy to help break old patterns.
Every large corporation has unexplored opportunities, potential for new growth and revenue streams, and surprising pockets of start-up minded talent, but senior management must be willing to embrace risk on the path towards invention. That’s hard to do. Instead, leaders of mature companies often focus on incremental improvements to existing products, leaving their businesses vulnerable to disruption.
Innovation requires a vision that borders on obsession to disrupt entire markets. Most of all, it takes trust – a willingness by senior management to let go and allow others - junior employees or outside consultants, product managers, engineers, designers - to experiment with ideas, building and iterating with users, and validating along the way before proving it’s foolproof on day one. But the potential rewards are enormous.
It also requires a financial commitment. Real change cannot be achieved without a serious investment so businesses must be willing to put their money where their mouth is.
Consider the on-demand fulfillment and warehousing platform developed by a global package delivery company to diversify its offerings. The company began by creating a kind of in-house accelerator at a separate location where a small team was free to explore new ideas in the burgeoning e-commerce market.
The team was separated from the main corporate structure to encourage creativity and prevent being hamstrung by organizational paradigms. It spent weeks considering and validating various opportunities before settling on one. It then pushed very hard to build and release its new service in just a few months. Enabling such entrepreneurial freedom and velocity paid off.
The result is a cutting-edge warehousing and fulfillment network tailored to the needs of business-to-employee e-commerce.
The platform leverages AI to analyze historical data and make predictions about future demand, enabling retailers to optimize their inventory and shipping schedules. It also uses AI to route orders and optimize warehouse operations, resulting in faster and more efficient fulfillment.
The company could have remained just a package delivery service but by leveraging its existing assets and exploring new opportunities, it successfully diversified its business and strengthened its position in the market. Instead of being outpaced by nimble competitors, it took the lead in this fast growing market segment.
One challenge of innovation is ensuring that employees are a core part of driving how an organization captures new growth opportunities. While a small team may be incubating a new business, the entire corporate workforce should be kept aware of and made receptive to what’s being done. If people work in silos, they will get left behind. And fresh ideas often come from unexpected places.
One key lesson is looking beyond the core business for growth opportunities and empowering untapped talent already on the payroll to help innovate and scale.
Take a major aerospace company with deep expertise in satellite technology. The head of its satellite unit saw an opportunity for a more robust revenue stream and invited external “business builders” to explore ideas. 6 months later, the unit launched a cloud-based, geospatial data analytics platform that gives developers and analysts access to satellite data, aerial imagery, and other geospatial data sources.
The new business has allowed the aerospace company to tap into the growing market for geospatial analytics and, today, it is a leader in the geospatial marketplace. The invention has not only expanded the parent company’s business horizons but demonstrated its adaptability and ability to capitalize on emerging trends.
By stepping outside of traditional models and building something new companies can recreate themselves rather than be left behind. In some cases, companies may need to bring in outside support - proven business builders - to work shoulder to shoulder with their teams to guide and accelerate the process. Ultimately, the goal is to give people the freedom to explore new options to help drive invention.
With such outside help, a food and agri-business company created a profit-for-purpose venture to improve the livelihoods of smallholder farmers in rural agricultural economies. The business provides smallholder farmers with an integrated set of services, including a credit facility, an e-commerce store for high-quality supplies, an advisory engine powered by machine learning, and an app for selling products directly. It has reached more than 150,000 farmers, with most farmers increasing their crop yields and incomes by as much as 25%.
These companies are just a few examples of how invention is disrupting industries. But why are these companies able to invent and disrupt, while others struggle? Most business leaders know the innovation playbook, but few live it with the right commitment, in terms of funds, in terms of experimentation, in terms of entrepreneurship.
One way that companies can foster innovation is through rapid building, testing, and learning from a minimum viable product. By quickly putting products out in the market, companies can gauge their audience's response and iterate accordingly, rather than adhering to long, in-house development cycles. A critical component of this innovation process is the integration of new technologies, including generative AI, which can enable businesses to create cutting-edge products and services.
To find their next light bulb, companies must embrace the idea of trusting "mini Edisons" – individuals who are highly focused, obsessed even, with building innovative products and taking risks - from both inside or outside the company. Passionate inventors should be given the freedom to operate and experiment, as their drive for invention can lead to significant breakthroughs and ultimately, success.
By fostering a culture that genuinely encourages entrepreneurial experimentation and risk-taking, companies can unleash the full potential of their workforce and remain competitive in an increasingly dynamic business landscape.
Disruption is not exclusive to digital or even AI natives. Traditional companies aso have immense potential for invention, provided they are willing to take risks. By identifying and empowering the passionate inventors, traditional companies can tap into new revenue streams, stay ahead of the competition, and continue to thrive.

title: Forget AI; Organoid Intelligence May Soon Power Our Computers
text:
While the world has been captivated by recent advances in artificial intelligence, researchers at Johns Hopkins University have identified a new form of intelligence: organoid intelligence. A future where computers are powered by lab-grown brain cells may be closer than we could ever have imagined.
What is an organoid? Organoids are three-dimensional tissue cultures commonly derived from human pluripotent stem cells. What looks like a clump of cells can be engineered to function like a human organ, mirroring its key structural and biological characteristics. Under the right laboratory conditions, genetic instructions from donated stem cells allow organoids to self-organize and grow into any type of organ tissue, including the human brain.
Although this may sound like science-fiction, brain organoids have been used to model and study neurodegenerative diseases for nearly a decade. Emerging studies now reveal that these lab grown brain cells may be capable of learning. In fact, a research team from Melbourne recently reported that they trained 800,000 brain cells to perform the computer game, Pong (see video). As this field of research continues to grow, researchers speculate that this so-called “intelligence in a dish” may be able to outcompete artificial intelligence.
Intelligence is broadly defined as the ability to acquire, store and apply information. This is one of the key defining characteristics of the human experience. Executing any task requires some level of intelligence irrespective of consciousness or self-awareness. An AI chatbot platform like ChatGBT, for example, can respond to its users in real time with curated responses, but the extent of its intelligence is bound by data-based algorithms. Computers inherently cannot “think” or “feel” on their own. Similarly, brain organoids can learn to perform tasks, but there is no evidence that they are capable of consciousness. When referring to artificial or organoid intelligence, we must be careful not to project uniquely human capabilities of thinking and feeling onto them. Intelligence alone is not sufficient for the subjective feeling of consciousness.
Both artificial and organoid intelligence, however, stand to be useful tools for increasing efficiency. Artificial intelligence can perform calculations, provide personalized recommendations, and facilitate automation of manual tasks. While AI can process information much faster than the human brain, it does have its limitations. AI technology is currently limited to sequential processing, and therefore, only excels at tasks that can be done in chronological order, such as mathematics. In addition to this type of processing, the human brain has the unique ability to perform parallel processing, allowing us to analyze multiple pieces of information simultaneously. Even with something as simple as the sense of vision, our brains can identify the color, shape, position, and reflective speed of an object instantaneously.
When encountering unfamiliar or changing information, human intelligence fairs far better than computers. A person needs far fewer trials to learn a new task. One study, for example, found that individuals were able to learn a simple” same-versus-different task” with only 10 training sessions. AI computers, on the other hand, were unable to learn the task, even after ten million training sessions. Not only is machine learning less efficient during complex tasks, but computers also have significantly greater energy demands. Estimates from 2016 showed that the equivalence of 34 power plants was needed to meet the energy demands of all data centers based in the United States. In contrast, the human brain with its undefined storage limit only requires a fraction of that energy.
By leveraging the benefits of biological learning, organoid intelligence has the potential to enhance automation and reduce energy consumption. Brain organoids provide insight into how the human brain performs complex tasks like learning and memory. This is only possible due to recent advancements in developing organoids that allow them to mirror the microscopic structure and function of the brain. These 3D models have been found to exhibit spontaneous electrical nerve activity and react to stimulation, in a manner that replicates brain activity recorded by an electroencephalogram, or EEG.
Where there is electrical activity, there is an active synapse, or a junction between neurons that allows information to be stored as a memory. The human brain has trillions of synapses that enable us to store seemingly unlimited information throughout our lifetime. To reach similar storage capacities, researchers aim to scale up current brain organoid models. In the near future, a computer powered by lab grown brain cells may be able to store and retrieve large amounts of data more efficiently with smaller demands for energy.
Brain organoid-powered computer systems may also provide a new window of opportunity for preclinical drug treatment trials. A biological-electrical interface can report real time physiological data on how nerve cells respond to a new drug, while mitigating the ethical challenges of exposing humans or animals to possible side effects.
Organoid intelligence has limitless possibilities for research and innovation. As this emerging field continues to advance, however, several ethical questions have yet to be answered. Currently, there is no evidence that these cells have a consciousness, or the ability to “think” or “feel” on their own, but as these models are scaled up, we cannot be sure that they never will. Consciousness is far more complex than we may ever be able to understand. It is possible that research will eventually encounter the Greely Dilemma: the idea that in an effort to develop more realistic and ethical methods for studying the brain, we may create models that are also eligible for moral and ethical protections. As these models become more “human-like”, researchers will be forced to define what makes a person, a person.
Even if these 3D brain cultures never become sentient, there is still the question of who owns the intellectual brain property that they produce. This is a question that has already been asked in relation to artificial intelligence. The fact that the stem cells used to generate brain organoids come from donor volunteers further complicates this ethical question. Do those volunteers retain the rights for anything created using their genetic code? While the field of organoid intelligence seems promising, ongoing research will require a close relationship between study coordinators, ethics experts, and the general public.
